failures.criterion: Architect's acceptance for this round: the per-address reread limit is derived from the shared bucket the process actually mounts, so no single unauthenticated address can hold the fleet's reread budget at zero and no deployment is tightened by a bucket it does not mount.
failures.evidence: At this head api.DefaultRereadLimit is one constant, {Every: 8s, Burst: 30}, derived from GCPRereadOverallLimit alone, while cmd/broker mounts that bucket only under gcp-secret-manager. Measured on the real binary, one address driven until its OWN bucket refuses (Retry-After carries the refusing bucket's Every): on an aws-secrets-manager broker, 33 rereads accepted and then 'Retry-After: 8' from the address's own bucket, against a shared bucket whose own refusals carried 'Retry-After: 1' — so an AWS deployment's per-address sustained rate is an eighth of the bucket it mounts instead of a half, a fourfold tightening (one write per 2 s becomes one per 8 s) for a Secret Manager quota it never touches. On a gcp-secret-manager broker the address's own bucket was never reached in 400 attempts, the shared 4 s bucket refusing 356 times first, which is the intended ordering there. Red test: packages/envoy/internal/broker/api/handlers_secrets_test.go, TestOneAddressNeverOutlastsTheSharedRereadBucket, in commit 3b4e444c. It pins the relation and not a number: it mounts a shared bucket of 1 s and one of 4 s through api.Register's real mux, drives one address past its own burst, and requires the refusal's Retry-After to be twice the mounted bucket's Every. Fails now: `cd packages/envoy && go test -count=1 -run TestOneAddressNeverOutlastsTheSharedRereadBucket ./internal/broker/api/` reports, for the 1s mount, 'one address's own reread bucket refuses with Retry-After "8" against a shared bucket refilling every 1s; want "2"', while the 4s mount passes. Verified fixable: with api.Register deriving reread.Every = 2 × rereadOverall.Every when Deps.RereadLimit is nil, applied to a scratch copy of server.go with a go build overlay and the repository untouched, both subtests pass and ./internal/broker/api/... stays green (67.6 s); cmd/agent-secrets's failures under that overlay are identical to its failures without it, all of them this sandbox's SO_PEERPIDFD and pty rows.

failures.criterion: The sizing rules state what a future change may safely do. A rule that walks a figure under the floor its own guard enforces, and a floor stated lower than the measured one, are both wrong in the direction that makes a change look safe.
failures.evidence: limits.go says the burst 'is divided by the replica count and not by its square' with a budget burst of 10, and that the agent-secrets row 'goes red at any burst below three'. Both are wrong, and together they are unsafe. Measured against the live row with a go build overlay changing only api.DefaultRereadOverallLimit's burst and nothing else (`go test -overlay … -run TestSecretDeleteAndRestoreAreServedByTheBrokerAtOnce ./cmd/agent-secrets`): burst 2 FAIL, burst 3 FAIL, burst 4 ok, burst 5 ok. The floor is four, not three — the row sends four rereads, not the three the comment describes (delete, restore, retag, and the NO_VALUE_KEY retag that expects the broker's no-current-value refusal and gets RATE_LIMITED instead when the bucket is spent; the burst-3 failure is that same step with the same message as burst 2). With the floor at four, the stated burst rule 10/N gives 5 at two pods, 3 at three and 2 at four, so the rule walks under its own guard's floor at the next replica count this deployment would ever reach, while the comment tells the reader that guard protects them. The shipped constant (5) is correct and the agent-secrets row is a real pin for it — it is red at 3 and green at 4 and 5, with no bucket of its own, exactly as the implement handoff claims — so what is wrong is the stated rule and the stated floor, not a value, and no red test of mine can pin prose. The pin that already exists is that row. The architect has ruled that the burst does not divide by the replica count at all.

proof.criterion: Both budgets cite a provider quota; the citation itself has to be right, not only the arithmetic.

measurementsForTheImplementer: oauthSecretTimeout headroom, which the architect asked to be measured rather than pinned: the two statements oauthstore.Store.Secret makes (insert … on conflict do nothing, then select) run from two sessions at the same moment against a fresh database, five runs, measured 2.7-6.3 ms for the contending session and 0.8-1.5 ms for the other. That is three orders of magnitude inside the 10,000 ms bound. Caveat, stated because it matters: this is psql against a one-row table of the same shape, not the broker's own call through pgx on the migrated schema, so read it as the order of magnitude of the contention and not as the call's whole cost. Nothing here comes near the bound.

The reviewer's second question — whether anything can pass policy.NewCurrent's ctx.Err() test and then block before the bind — is answered by case 1 above only for the parked load itself. Between that test and net.Listen the code mints a uuid, starts the listener goroutine and waits on firstListen, which is bounded by rereadListenWait; so the longest a signalled pod can sit there is five seconds, and it is not unbounded.

One residual, not a failure: with ONE signal and a store that never answers the first policy load, the pod waits indefinitely, because the ctx.Err() test runs after NewCurrent returns and NewCurrent runs on a context no signal cancels. It has bound nothing and is in no EndpointSlice, and a second signal ends it in 30 ms, so a kubelet's own second signal or its SIGKILL resolves it; recorded so nobody rediscovers it as a hang.
